Excavated and conserved brick remains answer different questions from that account; a modern photograph cannot show a complete ancient timetable.

subjects.summary: Mali’s rulers depended on a landscape of farming, fishing, making and exchange. The resources displayed by a court came through many people’s work. Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage is one dated episode within changing political networks, not the origin of West African urban life or its only important story.

subjects.geographicPrecision: Angkor Wat orientation within a wider group of capitals and settlements; no empire outline.

subjects.question: What is missing when a city is pictured as only a temple?
subjects.summary: Angkor was a landscape of temples, settlements, fields and water works built and altered over centuries. Stone monuments survive conspicuously; traces of less durable buildings and infrastructure require other ways of looking. Satellite observation, lidar, excavation and network models help us ask how the city worked, why it changed, and why the story cannot end with an empty jungle.
subjects.returnPrompt: What evidence would you seek about the people who maintained canals and grew food?

subjects.place: China; Northern capital at Kaifeng, later southern court

subjects.summary: Song institutions joined court service, commercial activity and skilled production. Northern and Southern Song had different capital settings, while neighboring states and changing borders prevent a single unchanging picture of China.

subjects.name: Inca weaving: skill across highlands and coast

subjects.question: How can the way cloth is made reveal connections?
subjects.summary: An Inca-attributed tunic joins skilled textile work to a larger question: how did households, specialists and state demands fit together? The finished garment and its broad date do not identify a worker’s obligations. Roads, stores, later accounts and household archaeology provide other evidence. They also expose differences between what authorities claimed, what people supplied and what particular communities could do.
subjects.returnPrompt: What does a piece of clothing reveal that a list of rulers might miss?

subjects.name: Voyaging to Aotearoa: knowledge at sea
subjects.place: East Polynesia and Aotearoa New Zealand
subjects.geographicPrecision: Destination-region locator; no exact reconstructed canoe track.

interval.note: Te Ara synthesis of arrival/settlement evidence. Not an exact first landfall or the beginning/end of Māori identity.

subjects.question: How can practiced knowledge leave evidence without a stone monument?
subjects.summary: Reaching Aotearoa depended on boats, provisions and learned judgment at sea. Archaeological dates investigate settlement; attributed accounts of teaching and practice explain knowledge that need not take the form of a written chart. Those sources have different purposes, and modern voyaging has its own history.
subjects.returnPrompt: What knowledge in your own community is learned through practice rather than a written manual?

subjects.name: Factory reform: a law and the work of enforcement
subjects.place: British textile factories; locator near Manchester
subjects.geographicPrecision: Regional industrial anchor, not a location for every inspector’s report.

interval.label: Act in 1833; inspector evidence in 1836
interval.note: Selected law-and-enforcement investigation, not the beginning/end of industrialization or child labor.

subjects.question: Does passing a law mean a workplace has changed?
subjects.summary: Textile production joined machinery with skilled tasks, household needs and children’s time. The 1833 Act created obligations and inspection powers; later records let us investigate their operation. Protection required evidence and continuing work, with results that cannot be read directly from the date a law passed.
subjects.returnPrompt: What evidence would convince you that a workplace protection actually worked?

subjects.name: A child in a cotton mill: photograph and caption

subjects.question: What does a photograph show, and what does its caption claim?
subjects.summary: A photograph, its caption and an inspection report reveal different kinds of work. Hine’s mill scene became part of a reform campaign; the caption reports an overseer’s denial. Later officials checked age evidence and inspected workplaces to apply particular rules. Neither the child’s age nor effective protection follows from the image alone.

subjects.name: Tomioka: adapting an industrial system
subjects.place: Gunma Prefecture, Japan
subjects.geographicPrecision: Mill-site locator within a regional production system.

interval.note: Opening event; the mill and associated techniques continued afterward. This is not an endpoint for Japanese industrialization.

subjects.question: What does it take to move a technology between places?
subjects.summary: Tomioka’s imported machinery depended on trained women, local building work and people raising silkworms. Later teaching, adaptation and storage extended the inquiry beyond the model mill; evidence of working conditions and legal protection needs its own dates and places.
subjects.returnPrompt: What local skills would a newly imported machine still depend on?

subjects.name: Haiti: freedom fought for in a plantation world
subjects.place: Saint-Domingue/Haiti, Caribbean
subjects.geographicPrecision: Gonaïves declaration-region locator; the revolution involved many places and changing alliances.

interval.note: Uprising to independence; not the end of the consequences of slavery or colonial power.

subjects.question: Who made freedom, and why was it contested?
subjects.summary: Enslaved people’s resistance broke the plantation order, but emancipation, control of work and independence were distinct struggles. Regional research, a leader’s letter and constitutional rules show people making different political choices. The 1804 declaration severed French rule while also establishing authority; it does not speak directly for every household.
subjects.returnPrompt: Why is the history of freedom longer than the date of one declaration?

subjects.name: Te Tiriti o Waitangi: texts, signatures and authority

subjects.geographicPrecision: Initial signing locator; sheets circulated to other places and did not reach every community.

interval.note: Document/signing chronology, not the beginning or end of Māori identity or agreement on every later interpretation.

subjects.question: What happens when two texts promise different things?
subjects.summary: Rangatira debated words, sought assurances and made different decisions as Treaty sheets circulated. The Māori text, the original English text and later translations need separate labels. Promises of authority and protection must also be tested against subsequent Crown actions.
subjects.returnPrompt: What would you ask before saying that everyone understood an agreement in the same way?

subjects.name: 1947: independence and the disruption of home
subjects.place: British India, especially Punjab and Bengal

interval.note: Selected transition; neither national identity nor displacement began and ended in one month.

subjects.question: How can political independence and personal insecurity happen together?
subjects.summary: Independence ended British rule and opened new political futures in 1947. Partition also divided Punjab and Bengal, separated neighbors and placed families in danger. Official plans, an annotated boundary map, a September telegram and later testimony tell different parts of the story. Read them together to understand how a change of sovereignty could coincide with uncertainty about home, safety and belonging.

subjects.name: South Africa: making rights a constitutional commitment
subjects.place: South Africa; Sharpeville signing context
subjects.geographicPrecision: Constitution-signing locality; a national political process extended far beyond this point.

interval.label: Democratic transition and final constitution, 1994–1997
interval.note: Selected transition:1996 signing and 1997 commencement are distinct. Not the end of every inequality or of the work of implementation.

subjects.question: What is the difference between promising a right and realizing it?
subjects.summary: Paul Weinberg’s photograph shows Nelson Mandela casting his ballot in the 1994 election. It records one person exercising a right in a transformed political system. The constitution-making that followed asked a further question: how could a government chosen by the majority be bound to protect dignity, equality and the rights of people who opposed it?
subjects.returnPrompt: Use one constitutional section to explain a commitment, then identify what evidence would test its effect in practice.

subjects.name: 1914–1918: a global war made by decisions

subjects.question: How did a European crisis become a war involving people around the world?
subjects.summary: A crisis became a war through governments’ decisions, military action and imperial power. Sustaining it required communication, factories, transport, food and care. Selected regional records reveal unequal participation and different household consequences. They explain how a global war reached ordinary life while preserving disagreement and gaps in whose voices survive.
subjects.returnPrompt: How can a map or poster make some participants visible and others invisible?

subjects.name: War, occupation and genocide
subjects.place: Europe, Asia and wider war zones; locator at Berlin

subjects.question: How did institutions turn prejudice and conquest into persecution and mass murder?
subjects.summary: Nazi Germany and its allies and collaborators persecuted and murdered six million European Jews in the Holocaust. Other groups were also targeted. War and occupation extended state violence across regions. This history requires attention to victims’ lives, decisions and institutions, rather than treating suffering as an anonymous total.
subjects.returnPrompt: Why should a history of victims preserve their lives and names as well as describe the crime?

subjects.name: Sputnik: a signal heard around a divided world
subjects.place: Launched from Soviet Central Asia, present-day Kazakhstan

subjects.question: Why can a scientific achievement also become a political event?
subjects.summary: Sputnik 1’s radio signal joined spacecraft, ground observers and competing institutions. Soviet planners simplified a delayed scientific project, then organized a launch that also drew political attention. A translated proposal, technical history and British parliamentary debate show different kinds of work and interpretation around the exact 1957 event.

Qin measuring objects announced central authority, while excavated wooden records show officials processing grain, reports and responsibilities in a conquered region. These sources let us compare what a government required with how an office worked. They preserve both coordination and constraint without making every official, worker or household identical.

subjects.summary: People provisioned households, built ceremonial structures, moved selected soils and returned to shared places. subjects.summary: Isfahan’s prosperity joined urban building, rural silk, skilled making, commerce and household work. New Julfa’s institutions developed after forced relocation. subjects.summary: A small walrus-ivory counterweight belonged to the technology of hunting at sea. Its curves and engraving connect practical work with careful visual design. subjects.question: How does clothing carry practical knowledge and identity through change?

subjects.name: Blackfoot bison knowledge and the work of a communal hunt

subjects.question: How much coordinated work lies beyond the dramatic moment at the cliff?
subjects.summary: A communal bison hunt joined preparation, coordinated movement and the work of making food and materials usable. Blackfoot collaborative accounts connect the cliff with camp, fuel, water, drying and later hide work. This selected landscape and later historical window do not represent every Plains society or the beginning of bison knowledge.

interval.label: Big Hidatsa village occupation, c. 1600–1845
interval.note: NPS’s selected village frame. 1845 marks relocation to Like-a-Fishhook, not the end of Hidatsa people, gardening or earthlodge knowledge. Other Knife River villages have their own different starting dates.

subjects.question: What changes when women’s gardens and houses are placed at the center of Plains history?
subjects.summary: Women’s gardens, houses and food stores helped make Hidatsa villages places of household work and regional exchange. Cultivation joined hunting and gathering rather than replacing them. Community-authored teaching and a named woman’s later recollections explain knowledge and authority while distinguishing Big Hidatsa from subsequent homes, displacement and continuing life.
subjects.returnPrompt: Compare this farming village with a communal bison-hunting landscape. Name a real difference, a shared need for knowledge and a limit in the evidence.

subjects.name: Kwakwaka’wakw potlatch: witnesses, prohibition and return
subjects.place: Northern Vancouver Island and adjacent mainland; locator at Alert Bay
subjects.geographicPrecision: Alert Bay is a cultural-center locator, not a border or a claim that every Kwakwaka’wakw nation shares one origin. 1921’s potlatch took place at Village Island.

interval.label: Selected legislation and cultural-center history, 1884–1980
interval.note: The 1884 legislation, effective in 1885, and 1980 opening of U’mista frame this inquiry, not the existence of potlatch or the end of return efforts. Prohibition was removed in 1951; practices continued during it. Later returns are not projected backward into 1980.

subjects.question: Can a government ban a practice without ending its authority for a community?
subjects.summary: In the public Kwakwaka’wakw accounts selected here, guests witness consequential family events, while preparation, food and gifts make responsibilities visible. Canadian prohibition attacked these relationships. Particular recollections and return histories explain why a law, a museum’s custody and a community’s authority are different forms of evidence.
subjects.returnPrompt: What is the difference between a law prohibiting a ceremony, evidence that people continued it, and a community deciding where belongings should be kept?

subjects.name: Ocmulgee: a council building, a revised date and continuing ties
subjects.place: Ocmulgee, beside the Ocmulgee River, present-day Macon, Georgia
subjects.geographicPrecision: Locator for one ancestral place, not a boundary for all Muscogee towns or the findspot of every dated sample.

interval.label: Earthlodge construction chronology under revision
interval.note: No settled construction/use endpoints are plotted. The older 1015 label is a median of early radiocarbon determinations; newer roof-wood evidence indicates cutting sometime after c.1160 and leaves possible earlier construction unresolved. Neither observation dates the lifespan of Muscogee people or the whole Ocmulgee site.

alternatives.label: NPS retains 1015, an older median date; this is not a directly observed construction year.
New roof-wood evidence indicates cutting sometime after c.1160; possible earlier construction remains unresolved.

subjects.question: How can a building bring people together while its history remains open to revision?
subjects.summary: People shaped clay, raised supports, stored food and made places for gathering at Ocmulgee. Surviving features, retained samples and current Muscogee perspectives make different parts of that history visible. A revised timber date changes the inquiry without replacing the building’s disputed case with an invented construction span.
subjects.returnPrompt: Choose one visible feature and one dating claim. What would you need to know before calling each ancient, reconstructed or uncertain?

subjects.name: Wendat village life: Jean-Baptiste Lainé and the problem of dating
subjects.place: Jean-Baptiste Lainé site, Whitchurch-Stouffville, Ontario
subjects.geographicPrecision: Site-area locator in southern Ontario, not the boundary of all Wendat homelands or the location of every later Wendat community.

interval.label: Preferred modeled village range, c.1595–1626 CE
interval.note: Manning and Birch 2022 prefer a model around 1600 over the older c.1500–1530 estimate. These bounds summarize a model, not directly observed foundation and abandonment years. The article describes probability ranges differently in its abstract/body; no single confidence percentage is asserted here.

alternatives.label: Earlier c.1500–1530 attribution relied partly on material styles and scarce European goods; the 2022 analysis prefers a later model.

subjects.question: What changes when a village’s date moves by about a century?
subjects.summary: A village depended on farming, building and relationships beyond one household. Public Wendat accounts explain that work and its political setting. A modern scientific graph asks a different question: when did this particular community occupy the Jean-Baptiste Lainé site? Its two calendar possibilities should not be mistaken for a century of continuous occupation.
subjects.returnPrompt: Explain why two peaks on a dating graph are different from a settlement lasting all the years between them.

subjects.name: Haudenosaunee diplomacy: Canandaigua, wampum and a promise
subjects.place: Canandaigua, present-day New York; six distinct Haudenosaunee nations
subjects.geographicPrecision: Negotiation-place locator, not the limits of Haudenosaunee lands. The archival document does not turn six nations into one uniform experience.

interval.label: Treaty signed 11 November 1794; U.S. ratification 21 January 1795
interval.note: The bounds connect two documented actions, not the founding or ending of the Haudenosaunee or the duration of the promises. Treaty text, ratification instrument and later community interpretation have distinct dates and roles.

subjects.question: What makes a promise between nations—and what would show that it was kept?
subjects.summary: Peace needed material work: protecting land, supplying goods, supporting skills and handling complaints. The Canandaigua document records commitments; Nation accounts explain speakers, wampum, cloth and continuing care. Reading these together distinguishes a promise from particular actions taken to maintain a relationship, without claiming that every commitment was fulfilled.
subjects.returnPrompt: Choose one promise in the treaty. What different source would help you investigate whether people acted on it?

subjects.name: Cherokee printing: language, political debate and forced removal
subjects.place: New Echota and southeastern Cherokee homelands; forced removal to Indian Territory
subjects.geographicPrecision: The locator marks New Echota’s printing and political context. It is not a single removal route or a claim that all Cherokee people left the southeast.

interval.label: Selected language/printing/removal inquiry, 1821–1839
interval.note: Sequoyah’s syllabary, newspaper publication and political reorganization frame the inquiry. The April 1828 image is not the February first issue. Forced removal from 1838 and the 1839 constitution do not mark the end of Cherokee people, language or printing.

subjects.question: How could a newspaper support a nation’s voice without guaranteeing safety or equality?
subjects.summary: A national newspaper required type, language knowledge, workers and money. Its pages also carried disagreement about who should speak and what to do under pressure. Reading print beside the constitution and a public Freedmen history shows Cherokee political agency without mistaking national sovereignty for equal rights or a newspaper for protection against forced removal.
subjects.returnPrompt: What does a newspaper page establish directly? Name one political promise and one experience it cannot establish for every reader.

subjects.name: Ojibwe manoomin: work, water and knowledge beyond a photograph
subjects.place: Great Lakes rice waters; archival photograph probably Ontario
subjects.geographicPrecision: Broad Great Lakes orientation point only. The LOC record says the photograph is probably Ontario; it supplies no secure lake or village identification.

interval.label: Archival photograph catalogued [1913]; a longer-lived practice
interval.note: The bracketed catalogue date anchors one document, not the origin or endpoint of manoomin harvesting. Later Ojibwe accounts interpret work, knowledge and continuity; they are not transcripts of the pictured person’s words.

subjects.question: How much work—and whose knowledge—lies outside the edge of a photograph?
subjects.summary: Food work extends beyond a photographed canoe. Attributed Ojibwe accounts connect gathering with drying, parching, hulling, winnowing and care for water. A specific U.S. treaty and GLIFWC’s later institutional account add political responsibilities without assigning their geography to the unnamed person probably photographed in Ontario. The picture, knowledge accounts and later environmental work answer different questions.
subjects.returnPrompt: Name two visible observations, one explanation supplied by Ojibwe accounts, and one question neither source answers.

subjects.name: Indonesia: a proclamation and a contested independence
subjects.place: Indonesian archipelago; proclamation at Jakarta
subjects.geographicPrecision: Jakarta is the proclamation locator. It does not represent the location of every struggle or the extent of Republican control.

interval.label: Proclamation in 1945; federal settlement in 1949; unitary state in 1950
interval.note: Selected revolution and constitutional transition, not the entire history of Indonesian nationalism or the end of all territorial disputes.

subjects.question: What had to happen after independence was proclaimed?
subjects.summary: A short proclamation in Jakarta on 17 August 1945 declared Indonesian independence in the name of the Indonesian people. Turning that claim into recognized and functioning government took years of struggle. War, diplomacy and disagreement over a federal or unitary state made 1945, 1949 and 1950 different milestones in the same unfinished political process.
subjects.returnPrompt: Choose one date and explain exactly what changed—and which question that date cannot answer.

subjects.name: Ghana: from organizing for independence to governing
subjects.place: Gold Coast and independent Ghana; Accra
subjects.geographicPrecision: Accra is a political and archival anchor, not a map of every movement or the boundaries of colonial jurisdictions.

interval.label: Political mobilization, 1948–1957; republic in 1960
interval.note: Selected route to independence and early constitutional choices. Earlier resistance and later Ghanaian history extend beyond this inquiry.

subjects.question: How did people turn a demand for self-government into a government?
subjects.summary: On a 1957 stamp, “Ghana Independence” is printed across an older Gold Coast design. The new words announce a political change; the cocoa workers and royal portrait underneath invite questions about what continued. Independence on 6 March 1957 followed years of organizing, elections and argument over who should govern, how power should be shared and what freedom should accomplish.
subjects.returnPrompt: Name one power that changed in 1957 and one kind of freedom that still needs its own evidence.

packs.title: Communities, cities and the evidence of work
packs.question: How do we know about early communities, work, exchange and political organization?
packs.orientation: Begin with things people made and places they built. A grain account, a tomb wall, a reservoir, a carved jade and a stone household preserve different kinds of human activity. Some societies built large cities; others organized life differently. Their histories are contemporary without forming a single ladder toward civilization.
packs.geography: Move among southern Mesopotamia, the Nile Valley, Gujarat, the lower Yangtze, coastal Peru and Orkney. River systems, arid landscapes and island settings invite different questions. The selected object’s place attribution is kept separate from the location of a wider society.
packs.limits: This is a selective investigation of archaeological and institutional evidence. Many communities beyond these places are absent. Large monuments and durable materials survive unevenly; they cannot stand for all early human life.

Americas.reason: Caral now has settlement, food-evidence and construction-renewal explanation with phased context. One Supe study and selected project pages do not complete wider American or household histories.

Africa.reason: The selected Saqqara wall now connects to a bounded source-based account of provisioning, Giza institutions and changing cult service. Wider Nile farming, households, gender and provincial histories remain selective.

Europe.reason: Skara Brae now has household/landscape interpretation, source-qualified phases and an original feature guide. Wider Neolithic Europe, measured plans and independent archaeological review remain open.

West/Central Asia.reason: Expanded Uruk account with distinct urban chronology, accounting diagram and source interpretation. Later residential evidence is not backdated; wider Mesopotamian and household histories remain open.

South Asia.reason: Expanded Dholavira water/work inquiry separates excavated components from proposed radar features. The regional seal has no asserted Dholavira findspot. Wider Indus reference history remains open.

East Asia.reason: Expanded Liangzhu account joins rice, waterworks and jade while preserving separate dates and corrected capacity estimates. Household relations and wider East Asian histories remain open.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: A sourced Kuk reference supplies a highland New Guinea agricultural setting from about 2400 BCE. Earlier C1 dates and mainland Southeast Asian settings still need research. The later Lapita dossier is a comparison, not contemporary C1 settlement evidence.

packs.title: Networks, resources and disruption
packs.question: How did regional societies interact, depend on resources and respond to disruption?
packs.orientation: Copper, tin, pottery, food and stories moved through particular networks. Communities also depended on landscapes, institutions and skilled work. Around 1200 BCE some eastern Mediterranean political centers changed dramatically. That regional investigation belongs beside other histories, with evidence for both disruption and continuity.
packs.geography: The main network case lies in Anatolia and the eastern Mediterranean. Move separately to the Nile, China, Mesoamerica and island Oceania. Earlier Caral and Dholavira contexts remain accessible where their occupation ranges overlap this window. Poverty Point adds a separate Lower Mississippi Valley investigation of earthworks, food and materials.
packs.limits: This chapter is selective. It does not establish one universal Bronze Age, a single cause of political change, or a global event in one exact year. European, inland South Asian and African regions beyond the selected Nile case need fuller accounts.

Americas.reason: Olmec and Poverty Point now have layered accounts, distinct phased contexts, geographic locators and material/source interpretation. These selected communities do not complete Gulf Coast, Lower Mississippi or wider American histories.

Africa.reason: Kerma-Egypt exchange and craft evidence; other African regions require separate histories.

Europe.reason: A sourced reference compares selected Aegean centres and British farms. There is not yet a standalone European dossier in this chapter; Uluburun remains a separately dated cargo comparison in West/Central Asia.

West/Central Asia.reason: Expanded Hattusha and Uluburun accounts distinguish capital phases, Gordion drought proxy, wreck association and contested tin provenance. These do not supply a full eastern Mediterranean or inland Asian reference history.

South Asia.reason: Dholavira’s later occupation provides an overlap with C1; it is not a full account of regional change after urban transitions.

East Asia.reason: Expanded Shang account separates the conventional period, Yin Xu late capital, ritual/casting practice and object-specific attribution. Household and wider regional coverage remain limited; no shared Anatolian collapse is inferred.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Lapita now joins pottery-making, provisioning and source-qualified island sequences, with a modern cast, original action guide and a correctly wrapped regional locator. Archaeological and linguistic reconstruction stay distinct; this is not a complete Pacific reference framework.

packs.title: States, ideas and everyday voices
packs.question: How did power, techniques and systems of thought change across different regions?
packs.orientation: Different materials preserve different voices. Royal texts, ritual objects, household work and portable images make an uneven archive. Compare the purposes and audiences of those records while keeping each region’s chronology distinct.
packs.geography: Move from Mesopotamia to South Asia, Athens and the Nile, then across Andean and island worlds. These are comparisons; no connecting line is inferred from contemporaneity.
packs.limits: Selected contexts offer depth rather than a catalogue of all empires or philosophies. Achaemenid, Greek, Indian and Chinese intellectual histories extend well beyond these cases.

Americas.reason: Chavín textile, Olmec and Colima material histories; not all American regions.

Africa.reason: Taharqo now has temple, production and funerary-labor explanation with a distinct phased context, original figure, inspected workshop photographs and local source-qualified references. Kerma offers a separately dated comparative bridge, not an unbroken polity or a complete African framework.

Europe.reason: Expanded Athenian account separates Archaic image, changing civic eligibility, public work and later constitutional description. Other Greek and European histories remain outside this bounded set.

West/Central Asia.reason: Nimrud now pairs royal imagery with a primary settlement claim, a later captive-provision letter and a licensed composite palace plan. These distinct sources deepen work and authority without completing Assyrian social or regional history.

South Asia.reason: Expanded Ashoka account distinguishes regional versions, audiences, practical instructions and unmeasured outcomes within a separate Mauryan frame. Wider South Asian coverage remains selective.

East Asia.reason: Expanded Qin account separates measuring devices, prescriptions, excavated Liye practice and their distinct dates. Broader Chinese institutions, households and intellectual histories remain limited.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Dong Son material and Lapita cultural traditions with uncertain functions and distinct dates.

packs.title: Contemporary worlds
packs.question: What did distant societies share—and which connections can we demonstrate?
packs.orientation: Around 200 CE, cities, farms, ports and households existed within many different political and cultural settings. Some regions were linked through specific networks of trade and movement. Elsewhere, a useful comparison does not imply contact. Begin with real objects, locate their date ranges, and ask what each can support.
packs.geography: Locate the Mediterranean, Red Sea, Central and South Asia, China, Vietnam, Mexico and northern Peru. Dots are regional or city locators, not boundaries. Objects retain their catalogue ranges, including later phases. Ohio’s Hopewell networks add an eastern woodland comparison without asserting contact with the other pilot societies. A separately dated Bering Strait object opens an Arctic inquiry.
packs.limits: An anchor year is a way into a changing world. This chapter is selective, especially for Africa beyond Aksum, South Asia beyond Gandhara and Oceania. Different evidence survives in different regions.

Americas.reason: Teotihuacan and Moche now add selected household, workshop and regional evidence, with original teaching guides and distinct reference histories. The earlier Chavín textile provides a focused annotated comparison rather than a contemporary case or proof of contact. Wider American histories remain selective.

Africa.reason: Expanded Aksum account distinguishes early Adulis exchange, changing royal writing and later excavated inland work. Africa beyond these selected northeast settings remains inadequately covered.

Europe.reason: Roman imperial representation; northern and eastern European communities need later expansion.

West/Central Asia.reason: Expanded Palmyra account separates family memorials, local civic regulation and caravan records. Wider Roman eastern provinces, Parthian/Sasanian histories and diverse households remain limited.

South Asia.reason: Expanded Kushan account separates coin catalogues, chronology disputes and temple maintenance in Bactria. The wider subcontinent, agricultural/household contexts and Buddhist institutions remain selective.

East Asia.reason: Eastern Han and selected tomb models; neighboring societies are not represented equally.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Đông Sơn material traditions; no Oceanian dossier in this pilot.

packs.title: Communities and institutions in transition
packs.question: How did institutions, beliefs and regional networks change after political transitions?
packs.orientation: Large political labels contain changing communities. Investigate how people made images, shared food, organized learning and built religious environments while political power shifted.
packs.geography: Capitals on the Bosporus, Tigris and in northern China sit beside Mesoamerican vessel traditions, South Asian monastic life and Central Javanese architecture. Chaco’s mid/late-ninth-century building context provides a distinct Southwestern case extending into the next chapter.
packs.limits: Western Europe beyond Byzantium, inland Africa, North America and many smaller communities need fuller treatment. The selected cases do not define one universal medieval stage.

Americas.reason: Maya text/food/rank and earlier Andean/Mexican contexts now include the beginning of Chaco’s regional building history. Most northern regions remain unrepresented.

Africa.reason: Later Aksum context reaches this window; no new dedicated sub-Saharan dossier for these centuries.

Europe.reason: Roman/Byzantine identity, changing political phases and devotional practice.

West/Central Asia.reason: Expanded Abbasid Iraq account separates changing capitals and authority, workshop evidence, ordinary wares and a later manuscript. Wider urban/fiscal/slave labor histories and the full region remain limited.

South Asia.reason: Expanded Nalanda account connects selected translated practices, resources and residential learning, retaining archaeological/conservation phases. The wider subcontinent and institutional history remain incomplete.

East Asia.reason: Expanded Tang/Chang’an account separates government, wards, translation, tomb representation and change. Wider East Asia and rural/tax/military household histories remain selective.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Borobudur’s Javanese monumental religious environment; island Oceania remains limited in this window.

packs.title: Cities, craft and knowledge in motion
packs.question: How were cities, trade, knowledge, power and everyday life connected?
packs.orientation: Skilled work and learned practices connect the histories of monuments, political institutions and daily life. Move between cities and voyages while asking which connections are demonstrated and which remain hypotheses.
packs.geography: The Sahel, Cambodia, China, the Andes and the Pacific receive new investigations. Byzantine and Abbasid institutions and Nalanda carry earlier histories into this window. Compare Chaco’s Southwest with Cahokia’s Mississippi floodplain; the companion investigation also visits earlier Poverty Point and Ohio Hopewell contexts. Ocmulgee adds a distinct southeastern river/council context, including Muscogee collaboration and revised archaeological dating.
packs.limits: Coverage of European cities outside Byzantium, Central Asian pastoral communities and many Indian Ocean ports is limited. Comparison does not imply direct contact among all selected cases.

Americas.reason: Expanded Inca case distinguishes textile skill, rotating service, resettlement, stores and a particular household excavation. Broader Americas and local labor variation remain selective.

Africa.reason: Expanded Mali case connects ordinary production, older urbanism, oral traditions, pilgrimage and a foreign royal image. Local administration, producers’ voices and wider African coverage remain selective.

Europe.reason: Byzantium’s changing institutions and 1204/1261 phases; other European regions need fuller dossiers.

West/Central Asia.reason: Abbasid continuation and contracted authority; no comprehensive Mongol or pastoral history.

South Asia.reason: Nalanda’s later institutional phases and archaeology.

East Asia.reason: Expanded Song case separates northern/southern government, seasonal lending, markets and ceramic evidence. Wider states, labor outcomes and rural histories remain selective.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Angkor infrastructure and Polynesian settlement/navigation provide distinct state and non-state inquiries.

packs.title: Connections, work and unequal power
packs.question: How did connections reshape work, belief, power and resistance?
packs.orientation: Ships joined ports through goods, money, stories and people. These connections were made by artists, translators, sailors and workers as well as rulers. Some were negotiated; others depended on conquest, enslavement and forced displacement. Begin in the 1450–1650 context, then follow selected consequences into the later eighteenth century. A companion investigation turns inland to Ottoman, Safavid and Central Asian cities and follows skilled work into later-eighteenth-century Iran.
packs.geography: Portugal, Benin, Kongo, South Asia, China, Manila, Mexico and Banda belong to different networks. The journey includes the earlier 1497–99 voyage as context and labels a Mexican jar made after 1650. Schematic routes do not establish a particular object’s itinerary. Istanbul/Iznik, Isfahan/New Julfa, Bukhara and the Shiraz political context add distinct West/Central Asian settings; a shared chapter does not merge their governments or identities. Makah Ozette, the Blackfoot hunting landscape at Head-Smashed-In and Hidatsa river villages add distinct northern histories. Southern Ontario and Canandaigua add distinct Wendat and Haudenosaunee investigations.
packs.limits: Selected African, Asian, European and American encounters, with ocean and inland investigations. This is not a complete history of Atlantic slavery, Indigenous resistance, the Indian Ocean, Ottoman Arab provinces, the wider Caucasus or Central Asia beyond the selected Bukhara case. Oceanian perspectives still need fuller treatment.

Americas.reason: Acapulco, Pacific cargoes and later Mexican ceramics; Indigenous and enslaved American experiences need fuller dossiers. Distinct Makah, Blackfoot and Hidatsa investigations add cedar work, communal hunting and village agriculture. Ozette burial estimates remain disputed; the selected hunting context is not the whole site chronology. An ancestral Wendat village and Haudenosaunee treaty diplomacy add northeastern histories. Modeled village bounds, treaty signing and U.S. ratification are different kinds of dates; no common polity or automatic succession is inferred.

Africa.reason: Expanded Benin and Kongo cases explain makers, religious translation and distinct royal evidence. Wider communities, collection histories and trafficking outcomes remain selective.

Europe.reason: Portuguese access and armed expansion; the VOC appears through Banda’s colonial records.

West/Central Asia.reason: Ottoman administration/workshops/markets, Safavid Isfahan and forced Armenian relocation, Bukhara’s urban/bookmaking contexts and later-eighteenth-century Iran now have distinct sourced dossiers. This is not an exhaustive account of Ottoman provinces, the Caucasus, pastoral societies or Central Asia.

South Asia.reason: Expanded Calicut encounter inquiry retains existing ports and intermediaries; broader Indian Ocean economies, local accounts and port histories remain selective.

East Asia.reason: Ming production and Pacific exchange; not a general survey of China, Japan or Korea.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Banda and Manila represent different roles in ocean networks. Oceania is not covered by a dossier in this pack.

packs.title: Industry, empire and struggles over the future
packs.question: How did industry, empire, resistance, mass politics, war, decolonization and technology shape ordinary lives?
packs.orientation: Three investigations connect work and machines, political promises, and war and technology. Begin with a photograph or document, then follow the institutions and choices around it. The chapter’s2000 boundary clips the view; it does not end ongoing societies.
packs.geography: Cases span Britain and continental Europe, the Caribbean and United States, Japan, Aotearoa, South Asia and South Africa. Companion inquiries add distinct Arctic, coastal, Plains, Great Lakes, northeastern and southeastern North American settings. Map locators do not reconstruct borders or photographic findspots.
packs.limits: Selective investigations, not a complete modern survey. Latin America beyond Haiti, China’s twentieth century, Middle Eastern national movements, African regions beyond South Africa and post-1960 computing need fuller treatment. War coverage explains major contexts and genocide without cataloguing every campaign.

glossary.definition: Support or commissioning of work by a person or institution, shaping what makers could produce.

glossary.name: tomb
glossary.definition: A place prepared for the dead. Its objects may reflect the beliefs and resources of those arranging the burial.

glossary.name: estate
glossary.definition: A substantial property and the land, buildings and labor that sustain it.

glossary.name: afterlife
glossary.definition: Beliefs about an existence after death. Historians study how people represented and practiced these beliefs.

glossary.name: evidence
glossary.definition: Information used to support or challenge an account of the past. Objects, written records and spoken testimony can all provide evidence. Each needs to be understood in context.

glossary.name: inference
glossary.definition: An explanation drawn from evidence rather than something directly observed.

glossary.name: chronology
glossary.definition: The ordering and dating of events. Dates can be approximate, disputed or revised.

glossary.name: ritual
glossary.definition: An action or sequence given particular shared significance, often repeated in a religious or social setting.

glossary.name: dynasty
glossary.definition: A sequence of rulers associated with one family; it is not the same thing as a whole society.

glossary.name: empire
glossary.definition: A political formation ruling over diverse territories and peoples, often through conquest and unequal power.

glossary.name: freedman
glossary.definition: A formerly enslaved man. The label identifies a past legal status, not the full experience of a person.

glossary.name: caravan
glossary.definition: People and pack animals traveling together, often carrying goods.

glossary.name: inscription
glossary.definition: Words deliberately written or cut on a surface. The author’s purposes and audience matter.

glossary.name: coinage
glossary.definition: Coins and the practices through which authorities issue and people use them.

glossary.name: provenance
glossary.definition: The documented history of an object, including its origins, past ownership and previous locations. Archaeologists distinguish this from provenience: the recorded location where an object was found. A find context also includes surroundings and associations. Knowing one part of this history does not fill gaps in another.

glossary.name: port
glossary.definition: A place where vessels land and goods or people enter a wider network.

glossary.name: stele
glossary.definition: An upright stone monument, often carved or inscribed.

glossary.name: archaeology
glossary.definition: Study of the past through material remains and their contexts.

glossary.name: irrigation
glossary.definition: Directing water to fields. The channels and their maintenance involve both environments and people.

glossary.name: tribute
glossary.definition: Goods or labor demanded by a political authority. Its precise form varies by setting.

glossary.name: iconography
glossary.definition: The study of imagery and its meanings in a particular context.

glossary.name: regalia
glossary.definition: Objects that represent office, rank or authority.

glossary.name: material culture
glossary.definition: Things people make and use, studied as part of social life.

glossary.name: enslavement
glossary.definition: The coercive treatment of people as property, denying freedom and exploiting their work.

glossary.name: colonialism
glossary.definition: Control of people and territories by an outside power, involving unequal political and economic relationships.

glossary.name: decolonization
glossary.definition: Processes of ending colonial rule; political independence did not automatically end every inequality.

glossary.name: archive
glossary.definition: A collection of records, shaped by decisions about what was created, kept, lost and made accessible.

glossary.name: industrialization
glossary.definition: Changes in production involving machines, energy, workplaces and labor organization; timing and effects differ by region.

glossary.name: earthwork
glossary.definition: A deliberately shaped construction of earth, such as a mound or enclosure. Its form alone does not establish its purpose or governing system.

glossary.name: terminus post quem
glossary.definition: The earliest possible date for an event, given the evidence. A timber could only have been used in a wall in or after the year its last surviving ring grew. The wood may have been stored or reused.

glossary.name: calibration
glossary.definition: Converting a radiocarbon determination into possible calendar dates using an independently established reference curve. One determination can have more than one plausible calendar placement.

glossary.name: syllabary
glossary.definition: A writing system whose signs represent syllables. The Cherokee syllabary is a system for writing Cherokee, not an ornamental version of English.

glossary.name: wampum
glossary.definition: Worked shell beads used in particular Indigenous contexts. The Onondaga account here explains agreements, speakers, memory and responsibilities; a pattern does not interpret itself.

glossary.name: ratification
glossary.definition: A formal act of confirming an agreement through a government’s procedures. It can occur after negotiation and signing, and does not by itself prove that commitments were fulfilled.

glossary.name: manoomin
glossary.definition: The Ojibwe name for wild rice, explained in the community sources as food with physical, cultural and spiritual significance. Related practices differ among communities.

glossary.name: winnowing
glossary.definition: Separating grain from lighter chaff, often with the help of moving air. It is one stage of finishing rice, distinct from harvesting, drying, parching and hulling.

glossary.name: marine reservoir effect
glossary.definition: Marine carbon can give a sample a different radiocarbon age from a contemporary land-based sample. Appropriate calibration and reservoir corrections matter; a regional revision does not automatically redetermine every catalogued object.

glossary.name: reconstruction
glossary.definition: A modern interpretation made from evidence about an earlier object, building or practice. It can help investigate how something worked, while remaining distinct from the surviving original.

glossary.name: radiocarbon
glossary.definition: A method that estimates the age of once-living material from radioactive carbon. Samples, calibration and environmental effects matter; an uncalibrated age in years BP is not automatically a calendar year.

glossary.name: waterlogged preservation
glossary.definition: Survival of material in persistently wet conditions that slow some forms of decay. The preserved material is still a selective record, not a complete picture of a household.

glossary.name: seasonal round
glossary.definition: An organized pattern of activities and movement through the year. Mobility can depend on detailed knowledge, planning and social institutions.

glossary.name: cache pit
glossary.definition: A prepared underground storage space. Its construction, contents and use require evidence; an explanatory model is not an excavated original.

glossary.name: repatriation
glossary.definition: Return of belongings or ancestral remains to the peoples or communities to whom they belong. The atlas follows the particular community account rather than assuming one process for every collection.

glossary.name: potlatch
glossary.definition: A ceremony with specific forms and responsibilities in different Northwest Coast communities. In the Kwakwaka’wakw account here, invited people witness consequential events and gifts acknowledge their role.

glossary.name: experimental archaeology
glossary.definition: Testing an interpretation by reproducing a material, technique or activity under stated conditions. An experiment supports a possibility; it is not a recovered ancient event.

glossary.name: archaeological tradition
glossary.definition: A research label for related material practices across places or times. It is not automatically the name of one people, language or state.

glossary.name: biomarker
glossary.definition: A detectable chemical or biological trace used as evidence of a substance or process. Its interpretation depends on the method, sample and alternative explanations.

glossary.name: kiva
glossary.definition: A Pueblo ceremonial space with varied forms and histories. Archaeological identification and living community knowledge both matter; not every circular room has an identical meaning.

glossary.name: proxy
glossary.definition: An indirect measurement used to investigate something not directly counted or observed. A lake-sediment signal, for example, requires interpretation before it becomes a population claim.

glossary.name: chiefdom
glossary.definition: An analytical term for a society with ranked authority and leadership above a local community. Its use for an archaeological case is an interpretation, not a surviving official name.

glossary.name: stonepaste
glossary.definition: A ceramic body containing abundant crushed quartz with clay and glassy material. It differs from porcelain even when makers adapt similar designs.

glossary.name: tughra
glossary.definition: A calligraphic emblem of an Ottoman sultan’s authority used on official documents and other media. Drawing and ornament could involve specialized makers.

glossary.name: forced relocation
glossary.definition: Movement imposed on people by authorities or armed power. Later achievements or privileges do not make the original movement voluntary.

glossary.name: caravansary
glossary.definition: An establishment offering space and facilities for traveling merchants and their goods, often linked to urban markets or overland travel.

glossary.name: madrasa
glossary.definition: An institution of learning in Islamic societies, with varied subjects, forms and patronage across time and place. A building does not by itself reveal every student’s experience.

glossary.name: lacquer
glossary.definition: A protective, often glossy surface finish applied over painted or decorated material. The Iranian case here uses painted papier-mâché and pasteboard.

glossary.name: sovereignty
glossary.definition: A claim to supreme political authority, including independence from another state. A declaration, recognition by other states and effective control can have different dates and histories.

glossary.name: federation
glossary.definition: A political arrangement in which powers are divided between a central government and constituent governments. Its actual distribution of authority must be read in the particular constitution or agreement.

glossary.name: Standardization
glossary.definition: An attempt to establish common units, forms or procedures. An announced standard and the way people use it are separate historical questions.

glossary.name: Dhamma
glossary.definition: In Ashoka’s messages, a moral and administrative program concerning conduct and government. Its uses need context and are not identical with a complete statement of Buddhist doctrine.

glossary.name: Deme
glossary.definition: A local civic community in ancient Attica. The late-fourth-century Athenian account describes scrutiny and enrollment of eligible young men among its members.

glossary.name: Stratigraphy
glossary.definition: The sequence and relationships of archaeological layers and features. An object’s manufacture date and the date or history of the deposit containing it are different questions.

glossary.name: Endowment
glossary.definition: A grant of land, property or resources intended to support an institution over time. Its terms and the work supplying that support need their own evidence.

glossary.name: Mit’a
glossary.definition: Rotating labor service required by Inca authorities. It differs from permanent or semi-permanent resettlement; provisioning does not by itself establish equal choice or returns.

glossary.name: Jeli / jeliw
glossary.definition: A Mande specialist in oral traditions and performance, with roles including genealogy, praise and diplomacy. Jeliw is plural; particular performances have their own dates, audiences and purposes.

glossary.name: Provisioning
glossary.definition: Organizing and supplying the food and other materials needed by people or institutions. Storage, preparation and delivery involve different tasks.

glossary.name: Shicra
glossary.definition: A woven plant-fiber bag. Stone-filled examples occur in Caral’s construction deposits; their presence alone does not establish how every worker was recruited or required to contribute.

glossary.name: Midden
glossary.definition: An accumulation of discarded material and occupation deposits. Its contents and layers can help investigate activities, but need their own context and chronology.

glossary.name: Temper
glossary.definition: Non-clay material, such as sand or plant fibers, mixed with clay to change how pottery behaves. Its composition can help investigate material sources, without identifying a particular carrier or voyage.

glossary.name: Type-site
glossary.definition: A place whose name supplies the label for an archaeological category. Similar finds elsewhere still need their own dates and contexts; the name alone does not prove that practices spread outward from that place.

glossary.name: LiDAR
glossary.definition: Light detection and ranging: measurements of light pulses used to model elevation. A ground-surface model can reveal forms, while excavation and dating help investigate their histories.

glossary.name: Faience
glossary.definition: A manufactured, usually quartz-rich material with a glazed surface. Ancient Egyptian and Kushite faience is distinct from a granite carving or ordinary clay pottery; a mould and production debris can help investigate its making.

glossary.name: Shabti
glossary.definition: A funerary figure intended to substitute for work required of the deceased in the afterlife. Its name, material, inscription and find context need their own evidence; a royal example does not represent every household’s beliefs.

glossary.name: Plain weave
glossary.definition: A way of making cloth. The crosswise thread (weft) passes over one lengthwise thread (warp) and under the next. On the return row, the pattern reverses. A diagram shows the method. Identifying the weave of a particular cloth requires examining its threads.

glossary.name: Residential compound
glossary.definition: A connected group of rooms and open spaces used for living and other activities. An archaeological compound may include production, storage and gathering; its walls do not by themselves identify one nuclear family or its legal status.

glossary.name: Find context
glossary.definition: The recorded place and associations in which something was found, including its position, surrounding material and relationship to other features. A regional style or present museum location does not supply a precise archaeological find context.

glossary.name: Relief
glossary.definition: An image carved or modelled so that forms project from a background surface. A relief can organize a story on that surface; its interpretation and use require further evidence.

glossary.name: Iconoclasm
glossary.definition: Opposition to or destruction of images, especially in religious settings. Byzantine disputes involved particular periods and policies; the term does not describe every Christian view about images.

glossary.name: Masonry
glossary.definition: Building with stone, brick or similar units. Facing stones and a rubble core can perform different tasks within one wall; its materials alone do not identify every builder or the institution organizing the work.

glossary.name: Workshop
glossary.definition: A setting or group in which people produce or prepare work. Size, training, ownership and the division of tasks vary; a catalogue’s workshop attribution does not identify every maker.
